lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Mr Crane. A moment.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Mr Bevan’s effects. His daughter has written for them. Box them up and send them by railway parcel from Paddington.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: And take this to Mr Dobbs at the Coal Exchange. Mr Hallam wants it in his hand today, not tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Paddington is not on the way to Lower Thames Street, Mr Grice.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Then you had better start walking, Mr Crane.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Thirty years at that desk, and they box him up in an afternoon.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Is that for the stove, sir? Bit small.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: No, Tom. It’s for later.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Nice watch, sir. Shame it don’t go.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Coal in August. Mr Grice says the damp gets into the drawings, and Mr Grice is always right.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Burn it? Not in here. If it’s what I think, I want it whole, and I want a coal man to see it.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Eleven years at this table. Other men’s mines, other men’s money, drawn very neatly.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Rain on Westminster. The clock tower is a grey ghost today. Good light for tracing, though, if you hold the paper flat to the glass.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: The Geological Survey’s map. A great black basin of coal from Pontypool to St Brides Bay, and the valleys cut into it like fingers.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Thirty years at this desk. He died at it on Tuesday, between one sentence and the next. Nobody has sat there since.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Half packed. Thirty years of a man, and room to spare.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: An empty tea chest from the clerks’ room. It still smells of Assam.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His field book. By rights it goes in with the rest.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: …No. Not yet.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His coal sample? No. That stays with me.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: She doesn’t need his pencils.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: The firm’s correspondence, filed by Mr Grice, by year, by client, by the will of God.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Personal effects go in the box, Mr Crane. Not on my desk.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Not to Grice. Grice would file it.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: The speaking tube to Mr Hallam’s room. You blow, it whistles upstairs, and Mr Hallam asks who has disturbed him.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: And say what? No.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: One empty shelf. Mr Grice will notice on Monday.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Levels, chains, and the good theodolite: a five-inch Troughton & Simms. Forty guineas, under lock and key.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Nothing in there I need now.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Locked. Mr Grice has the key, and Mr Grice has rules.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: I got a clip round the ear for that, sir. Worth it though.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Mr Bevan used to give me humbugs, sir. Now nobody does.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Life is hard, Tom.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: It’s harder without humbugs, sir.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Tom. A penny says Mr Pike wants Mr Grice in the strongroom. Urgently.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Mr Pike’s in Brighton, sir.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Mr Grice doesn’t know that.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: …Make it tuppence?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Pleasure doing business, sir.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Robbery, that is.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Mr GRICE! Mr Pike wants you in the strongroom, sir! Urgent!

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Mr Pike? He wasn’t in this morning…

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Very well. Touch nothing, any of you.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Now. Quickly.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: A pad of the firm’s blank chits. A humbug, which I’ll keep from Tom.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: My ventilation plan for the Ystrad level, signed off by Mr Hallam himself. He signs everything I draw. He’s never once read one.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His pen tray, his spectacles, a half-written letter.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: A lump of coal with a paper label. And his field book.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His daughter gets the personal effects. The firm gets nothing. That’s what Grice said.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His last letter, unfinished. She should have it.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His spectacles. One lens cracked.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: That’s everything that belongs to her. Everything personal, anyway.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Lid on. Twelve nails. Addressed to Mrs Gwen Rees, Pen-y-graig, Cwm Du, near Pontypridd.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: His notebook is not in it.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: The firm’s correspondence is the firm’s business, Mr Crane.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: He hasn’t looked up. He never needs to. If something called him away from that desk for a minute… Tom would shout anything for a penny.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Southampton… Ordnance Survey… here.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Mr Pike is in Brighton, Thomas.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Must’ve been Mr Bevan’s ghost, sir.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Ghosts do not shout up stairwells.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Government paper comes folded double, and the second leaf is blank, with the Crown embossed in the corner.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Letter to the glass, blank leaf over it. The light comes through the signature.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: “H. James, Colonel R.E., Director-General.” Slowly. Don’t stop in the middle of a stroke. Bevan taught me that.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: “The bearer, Mr E. Crane, Civil Assistant, is authorised to enter upon lands…” Any farmer in Wales would open his gate to that.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: I need Hallam’s signature to copy.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: I need Hallam’s signature to copy. It’s on the drawing on my table.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Hallam’s signature I have. I need something to write the order on. There’s a pad of the firm’s chits in my table drawer.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: A blank chit, the drawing behind it, both against the glass. “Please supply bearer with the five-inch Troughton & Simms.”

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: “R. Hallam.” The R is a fishhook, and the tail drags. There.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: The drawing can go back on my table. Nobody will miss it for a minute.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: The letter to Mr Dobbs at the Coal Exchange, by hand, today.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Mr Bevan’s personal effects boxed up for his daughter. The tea chest is by his desk. The firm’s papers stay here.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: That box to the parcels office at Paddington. The Post Office does not take parcels, Mr Crane, whatever you young men think.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Then the box to the parcels office at Paddington. The Post Office does not take parcels, Mr Crane, whatever you young men think.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Thirty years, and never once late. The firm sent a wreath.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: From the petty cash.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: From the petty cash, Mr Crane.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Instruments go out on Mr Hallam’s written order, and only on Mr Hallam’s written order. Signed for in the book.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Mr Hallam’s hand.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: The Troughton & Simms. What does Mr Hallam want with it?

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Surrey. Hmph. Mud.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Quite right.

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Sign the book.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: “E. Crane. One theodolite, five-inch, with stand.”

lines.speaker: Mr Grice
lines.text: Bring it back clean.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: “Cae’r Glo, below Pen-y-graig. Seam six feet. Tell no one.” I know it by heart already.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Cae’r Glo. Below Pen-y-graig. Pen-y-graig: the farm on his letter. His own land.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Six feet of steam coal, and he told no one. Not the firm. Not even his daughter.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Thirty years drawing other men’s mines, Josiah, and you were sitting on one.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: The night mail leaves Paddington at nine. Before then I need four things: what this coal is worth, a reason to be on other men’s land, an instrument to survey with, and the fare.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: All in my pocketbook.

lines.speaker: Crane
lines.text: Not where Tom can see it. He’d have it in his mouth before it left my hand.
